_source_note: Defect names and mechanism descriptions are paraphrased from the class definitions used in three public, verified steel-surface-defect research datasets. These are the REAL industrial defect taxonomy your synthetic CAPA scenarios should reuse, so your defect categories match genuine industrial terminology instead of being invented from scratch.

sources.name: NEU Surface Defect Database (NEU-DET)
sources.content: 1,800 grayscale images of hot-rolled steel strip, 300 samples across 6 defect classes

sources.name: GC10-DET
sources.content: 3,570 grayscale images collected from a real industrial steel-sheet production line, 10 defect classes

sources.name: Severstal Steel Defect Detection
sources.content: Real production-line defect images from a working steel plant, 4 anonymized defect classes

defect_families.mechanism_description: A network of fine, shallow surface cracks that form on the strip surface, typically linked to thermal stress or repeated stress cycling during hot deformation.

Foreign non-metallic particles (oxides, slag, refractory fragments) trapped inside the steel matrix during solidification. Some inclusions are loosely bound and flake off at the surface; others remain pressed into the material and only appear after rolling exposes them.

A localized region of the strip surface visually distinguished from the surrounding material by a particular characteristic (texture, reflectivity, or color), usually from uneven descaling or oxide formation.

A localized corrosion or mechanical-indentation pattern concentrated on a small area of the surface, penetrating into the material interior. Often linked to descaling effectiveness or roll-surface condition.
Oxide scale that was not fully removed before rolling gets pressed into the strip surface during the rolling pass, leaving an embedded scale pattern rather than a clean surface.
Linear surface marks (horizontal, vertical, or slanting) from mechanical contact with equipment, rollers, or handling surfaces during transport or finishing operations.
A half-circle-shaped material loss defect that occurs during shearing/cutting of the strip, typically from blade wear or misalignment in the cutting station.
Visible folds/wrinkles from excessive local deformation, generally associated with low-carbon material behavior under forming stress or die-fill issues.

A defect at the coil-to-coil weld joint (used when splicing strip ends for continuous processing); while a weld line itself is a normal process feature, a defective weld shows incomplete fusion, offset, or thickness variation that must be tracked and diverted downstream.

Low-contrast surface staining from residual moisture (drying step) or lubricant/coolant residue not fully removed during finishing. Easily confused with each other due to similar low-contrast appearance.
